mcqs.question: What extra step does a context switch between two different processes require that a switch between two threads of the same process does not?
options: Saving the program counter, which only processes have
Reloading the page table pointer so the CPU translates addresses using the new process's memory mappings
Writing the thread's stack to disk
Reassigning the PID, since threads don't have one
mcqs.explanation: Threads in one process share the same page tables, so switching between them needs no address-space remapping. Switching processes requires reloading the page table pointer (CR3 on x86) since each process has its own mappings. Both threads and processes have a program counter and a PID (threads share the process's PID); nothing is written to disk during a switch.

mcqs.question: A system is spending an unusually high fraction of CPU time on context-switch overhead. Profiling shows most of the concurrency is implemented as separate processes rather than threads within shared processes. What's a standard lever to reduce this specific overhead, where safe?
options: Move process-level concurrency to thread-level concurrency where the workload allows it, since thread switches skip the page-table reload processes require
Increase the number of processes further to average out the per-switch cost
Disable the CPU's cache entirely to remove cache-related variability
Switch every process to run on a single dedicated core with no other process ever scheduled there
mcqs.explanation: Thread switches within a process skip the page-table reload and largely avoid TLB invalidation that process switches pay, making them meaningfully cheaper — so consolidating process-level concurrency into threads where safe is a real, standard optimization. Disabling caches or adding more processes would make things worse.

mcqs.question: Why is the total cost of a context switch usually larger than just the microseconds spent inside the kernel's save/restore routine?
options: Because the kernel routine itself is poorly optimized on all major operating systems
It isn't — the kernel routine's time is the entire cost
Because the switch also triggers a full process termination and restart
Because after the switch, the new thread suffers extra cache misses (and possibly TLB misses) until its working set is 're-warmed', which is often the larger cost
mcqs.explanation: The direct register save/restore is fast, but the indirect cold-cache and TLB-miss penalty the new thread pays afterward — since the previous thread's activity evicted its cached data — is frequently the larger share of total lost throughput. No termination or restart is involved, and the kernel routine itself isn't the main cost.

mcqs.question: A system that normally does 50,000 context switches per second suddenly starts doing 5 million per second under a workload change, with no increase in useful work completed. What does this most likely indicate?
options: A healthy, highly responsive system making excellent use of its cores
The disk is the bottleneck, and context-switch rate is unrelated to disk performance
The scheduler is thrashing — spending a large fraction of CPU capacity on switching overhead rather than productive work, likely from far too many runnable threads relative to core count
The machine has gained additional CPU cores automatically
mcqs.explanation: A huge spike in switch rate with no corresponding increase in completed work is the signature of scheduling thrashing — too many competing runnable threads forcing excessive, low-value switching. It's not a sign of health or added cores, and while I/O-heavy workloads can raise switch rates, this magnitude with flat output points to thrashing.

mcqs.question: Why might spawning 50,000 runnable threads on an 8-core machine actively hurt throughput rather than just fail to help it?
options: It won't hurt anything, since context switches cost only a few microseconds each regardless of thread count
The OS caps runnable threads at the core count, silently ignoring the rest
The extra threads will all be blocked automatically to prevent this scenario

Far more runnable threads than cores forces aggressive time-slicing, and each additional switch adds both direct switch cost and a cold-cache penalty for whichever thread gets displaced, compounding into real lost throughput
mcqs.explanation: With vastly more runnable threads than cores, the scheduler must switch far more often, and each switch carries both its direct cost and an indirect cold-cache cost — at high enough thread counts this compounds into a real, measurable throughput loss, not a negligible one. The OS doesn't cap or auto-block runnable threads this way.
